headline: RFK Jr. returns to his old anti-vaccine group
summary: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. gave the keynote Thursday at the Children's Health Defense conference, the anti-vaccine group he chaired for years. He told the crowd it had "a strong and steadfast friend in the White House." It is the worst US measles year since 1991. Pennsylvania's governor said he should have urged people to get vaccinated.

cover_question.q: Is it OK to doubt vaccines?

cover_answer: The health secretary does. Nearly every doctor says no.
table_question: Is there such a thing as a bad question?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The country's top health boss gave a speech to a group that doesn't trust vaccines. Vaccines are the shots you get at the doctor, a practice drill so your body knows the germ before the real one shows up. Almost all doctors say the shots work and keep kids safe. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A practice drill for the body is the whole idea of a vaccine, and it isn't scary.

8-12.script: The government's top health official gave the keynote at Children's Health Defense, a group he once led that argues against vaccines. Doctors' groups say that talk makes parents doubt shots. Like a lifeguard saying life jackets might not work.
8-12.why: Speech to doubt to skipped shots to measles is a chain they can follow.

13-17.script: Is it OK to doubt vaccines? Kennedy says he is only "asking the questions" parents ask. Doctors' groups say the questions themselves spread doubt in the worst measles year since 1991. Where does asking end and undermining begin?
13-17.why: Teens know "just asking questions" from the internet.

5-7.a: No. Almost every doctor says shots keep kids safe from germs like measles. Nothing changes for you.

8-12.a: A group that argues vaccines are unsafe. Kennedy led it for years, then went back Thursday to give the big speech.
It's the worst measles year since 1991, with seven deaths in two years. Pennsylvania's four this year were all unvaccinated.

13-17.q: Is it OK to doubt vaccines?
13-17.a: Kennedy says he's only asking questions. He cut the childhood shot schedule, which a judge halted, and Trump ordered the MMR shot spaced out.
Andrew Wakefield, author of the retracted study linking the MMR vaccine to autism. Decades of studies found no link.
